title: Encoder downsampling and receptive field
goal:
Work out what the feature encoder of Section 2 and Section 4.2 does to the time axis.

Write two functions:

- `conv_output_length(n, kernels, strides)` returns the number of frames after a stack of unpadded temporal convolutions. One layer maps a length `n` to `(n - k) // s + 1`, and to 0 when `n < k`.
- `receptive_field(kernels, strides)` returns `(rf, stride)`: the number of input samples that one output frame sees, and the total stride in samples.

With the paper's kernels `(10, 3, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2)` and strides `(5, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2)`, the results are a total stride of 320 samples and a receptive field of 400 samples.
hints: Apply the one-layer formula once per block, feeding each output length into the next block. A single division by the total stride is not the same thing, because every layer loses `k - s` samples at the edge.
Track a running `jump`, the distance in input samples between two neighbouring outputs of the layer so far. It starts at 1 and gets multiplied by each stride.
Each layer adds `(k - 1) * jump` to the receptive field, using the `jump` from before that layer's stride. Start with `rf = 1`.
